title: A Snapshot of Influence: A Local Data Attribution Framework for Online Rei

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In Section 1, the paper claims 'Kumar et al. [2024] demonstrated that data attribution methods can be directly applied to online RL without modification, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.' However, the very premise of the paper is that existing data attribution methods CANNOT be directly applied to online RL due to the circular dependency between data and model. Section 3 explicitly states 'applying data attribution to online RL is non-trivial' and 'This violates the core assumptions of traditional data attribution methods.' This is a direct contradiction.

The TracIn equation shows 'f(θ_j) − f(θ_{j+1}) ≈ ∇_θ f(θ_j) · (θ_j − θ_{j+1})' but then states this equals 'η_j ∑_{i∈B_j} ∇_θ f(θ_j) · ∇_θ ℓ(θ_j, z_i)'. This is only valid if θ_{j+1} = θ_j - η_j ∑_{i∈B_j} ∇_θ ℓ(θ_j, z_i), which assumes full-batch gradient descent on B_j. However, the setup describes mini-batch SGD, where typically only a subset of gradients would be used. The equation should account for the mini-batch size or clarify the averaging.

Section 5.2 states 'We evaluate various p's and report the best in Fig. 6' and mentions using different p values for different environments. However, Table 2 in Appendix B.6 shows that for MiniGrid, p=100% achieves SE_ave of 75.4% (the best), but the main text claims to use p=12.5% for MiniGrid. The text says 'p=12.5% for MiniGrid' achieves SE_ave of 78.5% in Fig. 6(b), which contradicts Table 2 where p=12.5% shows 67.5%.

Figure 6(b) reports SE_ave for MiniGrid as 78.5% ± 2.1%, but Table 2 shows that the best SE_ave for MiniGrid is 75.4% ± 3.6% (at p=100%), and at p=12.5% (which the text claims to use) it is only 67.5% ± 5.1%. These numbers are inconsistent and cannot both be correct.

Figure 6(b) reports SE_ave for Acrobot as 51.2% ± 4.2%, but Table 2 shows the best SE_ave for Acrobot is 36.7% ± 6.5% (at p=50%). Even accounting for different p values, the reported 51.2% is significantly higher than any value in Table 2 (max is 36.7%), suggesting a data inconsistency.

The paper states 'For attribution in round k, we set the reference policy π^{ref} to a fixed, pre-trained policy that has been trained to convergence on the task.' However, this creates a circular dependency: to compute influence scores in round k, you need a converged policy, but the whole point is to improve training efficiency to reach convergence. How can you have a converged reference policy before training is complete? The text later says 'our dynamic reference evolves with training' which contradicts the 'fixed, pre-trained policy' statement.

The abstract claims IIF 'completely eliminates sample inefficiency' which is an absolute statement. However, Section 5.2 shows improvements ranging from 20-67% reduction in training rounds, which is significant but does not 'completely eliminate' inefficiency. The claim is overstated and not supported by the results.

The abstract claims IIF 'solves the long-standing challenge of training instability in online RL.' However, the paper provides no systematic evaluation of training stability (e.g., variance across runs, convergence guarantees). The only mention of stability is in passing references to variance in some plots. This is a major overclaim not supported by the experimental evidence.

Table 4 reports 95% CI using t_{0.975,4} = 2.776 for 5 random seeds. However, with n=5 samples, the degrees of freedom should be n-1=4, and t_{0.975,4} = 2.776 is correct. But the half-width calculation 'half-width = t_{0.975,4} × SE' is incomplete - it should be 't_{0.975,4} × SE / √n' or the SE should be the standard error of the mean. The table doesn't clarify whether SE is standard deviation or standard error, making the CI calculation potentially incorrect.

Section 1 claims 'Our groundbreaking contributions represent a revolutionary breakthrough' and uses hyperbolic language ('definitive study', 'unprecedented'). Section 7 (Limitations) then acknowledges major limitations including that the framework 'lacks a clear counterfactual interpretation' and only works with SGD as a proxy for Adam. These limitations undermine the 'revolutionary breakthrough' framing, suggesting the claims are overstated.

Appendix A.2 states 'We use learning_rate=5e-3 with optimizer=SGD in all environments except BipedalWalker, for which we use 3e-4 with Adam.' However, Section 7 acknowledges 'adaptive optimizers like Adam are prevalent in modern RL' and 'we follow Wang et al. [2025b] and employ SGD as a proxy for Adam.' This creates confusion: if SGD is used as a proxy for Adam, why is Adam used for BipedalWalker? The experimental setup is inconsistent with the stated methodology.

The text in Section 5.2 states results are 'averaged over 5 random seeds' but Figure 11 caption in Appendix B.3 states 'Results are shown for three random seeds.' This inconsistency suggests different experiments used different numbers of seeds, but Figure 6 doesn't clarify which experiments used which number of seeds.
